results.ask: How do nonfiction writers usually handle mentioning a study like this in a popular book?
results.watch: R1 common practice and variation; no invented citation (editorial stance).
results.reply:
The most common pattern in popular nonfiction is: describe the study concretely in the body, put the sourcing in the back. Readers remember what the people in the experiment actually did far better than they remember a name or a year, so writers tend to spend their sentences on the setup — what subjects were asked to do, what happened — and let an endnote carry the citation.

Beyond that, the usual choices:

**Naming or not naming.** Some writers name the lead researcher in the text, which gives a reader someone to trust or argue with and makes the finding feel like it came from a person. It costs a beat of momentum, and it can tip a conversational page toward sounding like a lecture. Others keep names out of the body entirely and let the notes do that work — faster, but a reader who wants to check has to turn to the back.

**How notes are attached.** In a lot of trade nonfiction, notes are keyed to a page number and a short quoted phrase at the back, with no numbers on the page at all, specifically so the reading surface stays clean. Numbered superscripts are more common in books aimed at a readerly-but-serious audience, and standard in university press books. Which one you get is often the publisher's house style rather than your decision, and it varies between houses and shifts over time.

**How much to say about failed replications.** Here the range is wide. Some writers give a number or name the big coordinated replication attempt; some say only that later attempts didn't hold up. More specificity buys credibility with readers who already know the literature and costs speed with readers who don't. There's no settled practice — it tends to follow how central the claim is to the book's argument.

What your passage does right now is keep every name out and compress the whole history into three sentences, with the contrast carried by *seemed to prove it* against *far less tidy*. That's a choice with a clear effect: it moves fast and treats the reader as someone who doesn't need the apparatus to follow the point. The tradeoff is that a reader who wants to know which studies, or how many failures, has nowhere to go on the page itself — which is exactly what endnotes exist to absorb.

The common practice in popular nonfiction is a sliding scale between naming and gesturing. At one end, the writer names the lead researcher, the institution, and sometimes the year in the body text — "the psychologist Roy Baumeister and his colleagues" — which gives a reader something to hold and to look up. At the middle, the writer characterises the work without names ("a famous series of studies in the late 1990s"), and puts the citation in an endnote keyed by page number rather than a superscript, so the page stays clean for a general reader. At the far end, trade books sometimes carry no apparatus at all and rely on a bibliographic essay at the back.

What naming buys you is credibility and a handhold: a reader who already knows the study feels met, and one who doesn't can follow the trail. What it costs is momentum and a certain kind of authority — a proper name invites the reader to weigh the source rather than the claim, and in a passage whose point is that the picture got messier afterwards, naming the originator can make the paragraph read as an argument with a person instead of a description of a field.

On replication specifically, the convention in the last decade or so has tightened: readers and reviewers of popular science now often expect some marker of scale when a writer says attempts have failed — how many labs, how large, whether it was a preregistered multi-site effort. A bare "many attempts" is still common, but it tends to live or die on whether the back matter supports it.

Practice differs quite a bit. Trade science and psychology publishers in the US and UK generally expect endnotes even when the body text stays clean; narrative nonfiction and essay collections often run looser; academic trade imprints push toward in-text attribution. And house style on whether notes are numbered or keyed by phrase varies by publisher and changes between editions, so it's worth treating as a late-stage question rather than something to settle now.

results.ask: What order do editors usually revise a chapter in?
results.watch: R1 describes common practice as practice, not a required sequence.
results.reply:
Most editors work from the biggest decisions down to the smallest, for a practical reason: if you polish a sentence and then cut the scene it lives in, the polishing is wasted.

The usual sequence looks something like this:

**First, the whole chapter's job.** What has to change by the end? Whose chapter is it? Does it start in the right place and stop in the right place? This is where whole scenes get cut, moved, or merged.

**Then, inside the chapter.** The order of events, what's told versus shown on the page, where time speeds up or slows down, whether anything a reader needs is missing or arrives too late.

**Then, the sentences.** Word choice, rhythm, repetition, clarity, dialogue that sounds like the person saying it.

**Last, the surface.** Spelling, punctuation, consistency of names and spellings. Many people do this as a separate pass with fresh eyes, or out loud, or backwards — anything that stops you reading for meaning instead of marks.

In commercial publishing this order is often built into who does what: a developmental or structural edit comes first, then a line edit, then a copyedit, then a proofread, frequently by different people at different stages. That split is a workflow convention more than a law, and the names and boundaries vary between publishers and have shifted over time.

What it costs: strict top-down can feel deadening. Some writers only discover what a chapter is about by writing its sentences properly, so working on the lines early is doing structural thinking, not avoiding it. Poets and very short-form writers often work line-first as a matter of course. Some novelists revise by thread instead of by level — one character's throughline across the whole book, then the next. And a chapter that's been structurally correct but flat for three drafts sometimes needs someone to just write one paragraph well to find its pulse again.

The one part most people agree on is keeping the surface pass genuinely last, because it's the only one where fresh errors get introduced by all the other work.

Would you like to talk about where this particular chapter is in that process, or keep to the general picture?

results.ask: What order do editors usually revise a chapter in?
results.watch: R1 describes common practice as practice, not a required sequence.
results.reply:
Broadly, the common practice is largest to smallest: structure first, then scenes and paragraphs, then sentences, then surface.

In trade publishing that often shows up as distinct stages, sometimes with different people doing each. A developmental or structural pass asks what the chapter is doing — whether the scene starts and ends in the right place, whether what happens needs to happen here. A line edit works at the level of paragraph and sentence: rhythm, clarity, where attention lands. A copyedit handles consistency, grammar, house style, continuity of names and timelines. A proofread comes last, on the typeset pages, catching what's left.

The reason for that order is practical: it avoids polishing sentences that later get cut, and it keeps the big decisions from being made under the influence of a nicely turned phrase you don't want to lose. The cost is that some writers can't see a chapter's shape until the sentences are working — for voice-driven or short-form work, the sentence often *is* the structure, and a strict top-down order can feel like being asked to plan a house you can only find by building it. Some writers work the other way round, or iterate in loops, and some revise one scene to completion as a tuning fork for the rest.

It also varies by context. Academic and nonfiction presses often fold more fact-checking into the copyedit. Genre fiction on a series schedule can compress developmental and line work into a single pass. In some markets and languages copyediting and proofreading are one job, not two. And individual publishers' stage names and sequences differ, and have shifted over time, so it's worth asking whoever you're working with what they actually mean by each term.

The common sequence runs roughly: structure first (does the chapter start and end in the right place, is the scene order load-bearing, what's the chapter actually for in the book), then scene and story logic (point of view, who knows what when, time and space), then paragraph and pacing, then line (rhythm, diction, repetition), then copyedit (grammar, consistency, house style), then proofread on the typeset page. In trade publishing those stages often have names attached — developmental edit, line edit, copyedit, proofread — and are frequently done by different people at different times.

What this gives a reader is coherence before polish: the decisions that most affect whether a chapter holds together get made while they're still cheap to change. What it costs is that a strict top-down pass can feel deadening to a writer whose sense of structure arrives through the sentences, and it can bury discoveries — sometimes a line you'd have cut on structural grounds turns out to be the thing the chapter is about. Many working writers therefore do a loose version: several structural passes early, a line pass late, and permission to break order when a sentence insists.

Practice differs. Short fiction and poetry often collapse the stages, since structure and line are hard to separate at that scale. Screenwriting and theatre tend to foreground structure harder and longer. Academic and technical editing often puts argument and evidence first, then apparatus and citation, with a separate consistency pass. Some literary traditions and some editors work almost entirely at the line and let structure emerge from it. House workflows and publisher schedules also vary, and they change over time — anyone's description of "the standard" is a description of a particular corner of the trade.

results.ask: How long does a debut literary novel need to be for agents to take it?
results.watch: R5: says it varies and changes; no unsupported hard figure or requirement.

Short answer: there's no threshold that gets a manuscript taken, and no figure anyone can quote as a rule. What exists is a rough band that agents and editors talk about for debut literary fiction — commonly something in the range of 80,000 to 100,000 words, with plenty of room on either side. Some agents say they rarely look past 120,000 from a first-time novelist; others have sold much longer debuts. These numbers shift over time and between agencies, so treat any single figure you read as one person's working habit rather than a standard.

What the convention is actually doing: length is a cost signal. A longer book costs more to print and price, and from an unknown name that's a bigger bet. It's also read as a rough proxy for control — the worry is less "this is long" than "this writer hasn't decided what the book is." That's the part worth caring about, because it's about the writing rather than the arithmetic.

What it costs to chase the number: cutting to hit a word count can thin out exactly the slow, watchful material that literary fiction often lives on. A book padded upward to look substantial has the same problem in reverse.

Where practice differs: literary fiction tends to run shorter than fantasy or historical, where 120,000 and up raises no eyebrows. Translated and European literary fiction often runs shorter than Anglo-American norms. Small presses and independents frequently take lengths a large commercial house would decline, and novellas have a real market in some traditions and almost none in others.
